doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Learning small-group horn writing from Duke Ellington
summary: A bass player lent him a late-1930s Ellington small-group album, and he borrowed the idea of three horns sounding like a wall of sound.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah. Oh and idea I got from that minimalist thing of getting a little bit to sound like a lot was a bass player we worked with years ago with an old incarnation of this band, Dave Lanyardo. He lent me this album and it was late 30s sort of Duke Ellington, small group stuff. I was never into that big band game really, but this was Duke Ellington with Rex Stewart and Johnny Hodges was it.

Yeah. And it’s a small three horn — what do you call it — section with just a basic rhythm section underneath, bass, drums, piano. And the amount of stuff they’d get up to with that, you know. Two of them would keep this little harmonized vamp going on, and one would be out front soloing, and then when he steps back in and they change it when another one steps out to solo. And they modify the thing to suit what the remaining two instruments are playing. And I thought that’s a way, it sounds like a big wall of sound but there’s only three horns playing. And I think I nicked the idea from that.
That’s great. You have to know what notes to pick I think.
